title: js backend: numeric `FixedArray`s other than `Byte` are plain `Array`s; typed arrays measure 2–2.8× faster
body:
Follow-up to #646 (closed as not planned while waiting for a use case). Two use cases with numbers.

## What the js backend emits (moonc v0.10.21+06da1ed44)

| MoonBit type | js representation |
|---|---|
| `FixedArray[Byte]`, `Bytes` | `Uint8Array` (`$makebytes`) |
| `FixedArray[Double]`, `FixedArray[UInt]`, `FixedArray[Int]` | `new Array(n)` then `.fill(v)` (`$make_array_len_and_init`) |

`UInt` values are held as signed numbers (`0xFFFFFFFFU` is `-1`), so a library cannot substitute a `Uint32Array` through `extern "js"` safely: values of 2^31 and above read back as different numbers and `==` no longer matches.

## 1. Minimal loop

```moonbit
let n = 1 << 20
let fa = FixedArray::makei(n, i => ((i * 7919 + 13) % 1021).to_double() / 512.0 - 1.0)
let fb = FixedArray::makei(n, i => (((i + 1) * 7919 + 13) % 1021).to_double() / 512.0 - 1.0)
for i in 0..<n {
  fa[i] = fa[i] * 0.999 + fb[i]
}
```

The same loop on two `Float64Array`s made through `extern "js"` (`(n) => new Float64Array(n)`, `(a, i) => a[i]`, `(a, i, v) => { a[i] = v }`). `moon bench --release --target js`, pinned to one core, two runs of 10 batches:

| | run 1 | run 2 | min over both runs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FixedArray[Double]` | 3.15 ± 1.99 ms | 2.69 ± 1.12 ms | 2.09 ms |
| `Float64Array` | 1.14 ± 0.22 ms | 1.23 ± 0.20 ms | 0.95 ms |

2.2–2.8× faster by mean, 2.2× by minimum, and much steadier.

## 2. A compression encoder's hash table

A Brotli encoder (quality 9) allocates a hash table of `FixedArray[UInt]` per stream and reads and writes it once or more per input byte. Allocating it as a `Uint32Array` instead took encoding a 64 KiB text from 53.6 to 30.4 ms on js (median of five runs per side). We did not ship it, because of the representation mismatch above.

## Request

Represent `FixedArray[Double]`, `FixedArray[Float]` and the integer `FixedArray`s as the matching typed arrays on js, as `FixedArray[Byte]` already is; or, if that is not planned, document the representation so that libraries can rely on it in `extern "js"` code.

Not every numeric workload gains: an FFT kernel (several operations per element, small working set) measured within ±10% either way, the size of its run-to-run spread. The gain shows in streaming loops and large tables.

Environment: moon/moonrun 0.1.20261117, node v26.13.1, Linux x86-64 (Intel Core i5-10400F).

title: moon-lsp stops reading requests after an input decoding exception
body:
`moonbitlang/moonbit-compiler` has issues disabled and there is no separate
language-server repository, so I am reporting this here (same path as #1328,
#1372). The behaviour is in `moon-lsp`, not in `moonc` or `core`.

## Summary

After a successful `initialize` / `initialized` exchange, four malformed inputs
leave `moon-lsp` alive but unresponsive over stdio: scalar `params`, a `[1,2]`
body, a `{,}` body, and a UTF-8 BOM before `Content-Length`. In each case the
process stayed alive with stdout open and no output, and two later complete
requests stayed unread in the stdin pipe for 15 s.

## Environment

`moon 0.1.20261104 (940aa18)`, `moonc v0.10.20+65efd5b93`, Linux x86_64.
`moon-lsp` sha256 `5b9f19e9…2f8801d`. The reproductions do not invoke `moonc`,
so this is not a compiler ICE.

## Reproduction

Start `moon-lsp --stdio`, handshake, send one trigger, then a complete request.

| trigger | bytes sent | stderr |
|---|---|---|
| A scalar `params` | `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"textDocument/hover","params":null}` | `invalid structured value` (`Packet.t_of_fields`) |
| B non-object body | `Content-Length: 5\r\n\r\n[1,2]` | `invalid packet` (`Packet.t_of_yojson`) |
| C BOM before header | `\xef\xbb\xbf` + a valid `shutdown` frame | `content length absent` (`Io.Make.read_header`) |
| D invalid JSON body | `Content-Length: 3\r\n\r\n{,}` | `Yojson.Json_error` (lexer) |

```python
import json, os, select, subprocess, time
p = subprocess.Popen([os.path.expanduser("~/.moon/bin/moon-lsp"), "--stdio"],
                     stdin=subprocess.PIPE, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE)
def raw(b): p.stdin.write(b); p.stdin.flush()
def obj(o):
    b = json.dumps(o).encode(); raw(b"Content-Length: %d\r\n\r\n" % len(b) + b)
def drain(s):
    out, end = b"", time.time() + s
    while time.time() < end:
        if select.select([p.stdout], [], [], 0.05)[0]:
            c = os.read(p.stdout.fileno(), 65536)
            if not c: break
            out += c
    return out
try:
    obj({"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize",
         "params":{"processId":None,"rootUri":None,"capabilities":{}}}); drain(3)
    obj({"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"initialized","params":{}})
    raw(b"Content-Length: 5\r\n\r\n[1,2]")            # B; swap in A, C or D
    time.sleep(0.1)
    obj({"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"shutdown","params":{}})
    print(len(drain(2)), p.poll() is None)           # 0 True
finally:
    p.kill(); p.wait()
```

## Actual

All four triggers: no response to the trigger, none to the follow-up, process
alive, CPU ~0%, stdout open (`EAGAIN`, not EOF). `FIONREAD` on the pipe showed
**254 bytes** unread — exactly the two follow-up frames — versus 0 before the
trigger and 0 in a control session that answered them.

Controls all answer normally: `params: {}` and `params: []` → `-32602`,
`params` omitted → `-32602 params are required`, unknown method with `{}` →
`-32601`, well-formed `hover` params → `result: null`.

Full stderr for B:

```
| Internal error: Uncaught exception.
| Jsonrpc: json conversion failed: invalid packet
| Called from Jsonrpc.Packet.t_of_yojson in ocaml-lsp/jsonrpc/src/jsonrpc.ml, line 291
| Called from Lsp__Io.Make.read in ocaml-lsp/lsp/src/io.ml, line 103
```

The exceptions are raised at different call sites inside the bundled ocaml-lsp
(`Packet.t_of_fields`, `Packet.t_of_yojson`, the Yojson lexer,
`Io.Make.read_header`), and all four escape `Lsp__Io.Make.read`. So these are
grouped by symptom, not by an established common root cause. I do not know the
bundled dependency revision, so I do not claim which layer should catch it.

## Expected

A → `-32600`/`-32602`; B → `-32600` (batch-aware implementations may report two
errors); D → `-32700`; C → closing the connection is also reasonable. In every
case the session should recover or close, not stay alive with input unread.
JSON-RPC 2.0 requires a response to every request and restricts `params` to an
object or array.

## Additional

- Impact: later requests on the connection got no response during the
  observation window, so editor features using it may stop until restart.
- Trigger A is realistic: Emacs 29 Eglot sends `params: null` for `shutdown`
  ([call](https://github.com/emacs-mirror/emacs/blob/emacs-29/lisp/progmodes/eglot.el#L923),
  [encoding](https://github.com/emacs-mirror/emacs/blob/emacs-29/lisp/jsonrpc.el#L501)).
- #1372 is a different defect (100% CPU spin inside `format-nth`).
  [ocaml-lsp#1330](https://github.com/ocaml/ocaml-lsp/issues/1330) is a related
  precedent — string `params` caused a `missing field error` and the server
  died — but not the same raising site or failure mode.

## Not established

Root cause; recovery after the 15 s window; whether every method is affected
(`hover` was tested with all four scalar types, `shutdown` and an unknown method
with `null`); behaviour of the Wasm build.

title: moon-lsp hangs at 100% CPU in format-nth when the last top-level block has no trailing newline
body:
## moon-lsp hangs at 100% CPU in `format-nth` when the last top-level block has no trailing newline

### Summary

The `moonbit-lsp/format-nth` request never returns, and moon-lsp spins at 100% CPU, when it formats the **last** top-level block of a file that does **not** end with a newline. The server stays stuck until it is killed, and every later request (hover, completion, diagnostics) hangs behind it.

In VS Code this is triggered by **Update test** (code lens / Test Explorer). When the `moon test --update` run finishes, the extension sends `format-nth` for the test's block. If that test is the last one in a file with no final newline, the server hangs.

### Minimal reproduction

The request on its own reproduces it. No project or open document is needed.

`hang.json` (never returns):

```json
{"content": "fn f() -> Unit {\n  ()\n}", "n": 0, "isMarkdown": false}
```

`ok.json` (identical except for the trailing `\n`; returns immediately):

```json
{"content": "fn f() -> Unit {\n  ()\n}\n", "n": 0, "isMarkdown": false}
```

Script that starts moon-lsp over stdio, sends `initialize` then `moonbit-lsp/format-nth` with the given params, and waits 10 s for the response:

<details>
<summary>replay.py</summary>

```python
import json, os, select, subprocess, sys, time

req = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
p = subprocess.Popen([os.path.expanduser('~/.moon/bin/moon-lsp'), '--stdio'],
                     stdin=subprocess.PIPE, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)

def send(m):
    b = json.dumps(m).encode()
    p.stdin.write(b'Content-Length: %d\r\n\r\n' % len(b) + b)
    p.stdin.flush()

def recv(want, timeout):
    end = time.time() + timeout
    while time.time() < end:
        r, _, _ = select.select([p.stdout], [], [], 0.2)
        if not r:
            continue
        line = p.stdout.readline()
        if line.startswith(b'Content-Length'):
            n = int(line.split(b':')[1])
            while p.stdout.readline().strip():
                pass
            m = json.loads(p.stdout.read(n))
            if m.get('id') == want:
                return m
    return None

send({'jsonrpc': '2.0', 'id': 1, 'method': 'initialize',
      'params': {'processId': None, 'rootUri': None, 'capabilities': {}}})
recv(1, 10)
send({'jsonrpc': '2.0', 'method': 'initialized', 'params': {}})
send({'jsonrpc': '2.0', 'id': 2, 'method': 'moonbit-lsp/format-nth', 'params': req})
r = recv(2, 10)
print('HUNG (no response in 10s)' if r is None
      else 'OK: ' + json.dumps(r.get('result', r.get('error')))[:300])
p.kill()
```

</details>

```
$ python3 replay.py hang.json
HUNG (no response in 10s)
$ python3 replay.py ok.json
OK: {"newText": "///|\nfn f() -> Unit {\n  ()\n}\n", "range": ...}
```

### Observations

- A trailing newline is the only difference between the hanging and the working request.
- Only the last block is affected. In the multi-block file where I first hit this, formatting block `n = 4` of 6 worked, while `n = 5` (the last block) hung.
- It does not depend on the block's contents. A `test` block with a multi-line `debug_inspect` snapshot and a trivial `fn` both hang. Adding or removing a `///|` separator before the block makes no difference.
- `moon fmt` on the command line formats the same file correctly. Only the LSP's single-block formatter is affected.

### Stack while hung

From macOS `sample` on the stuck process. The main thread is always in the same loop:

```
on_request
  format_nth
    format_nth_impl_from_source
      pretty
        skip_until            <- loops forever
          peek_inner / peek_nth / skip / pos_compare
```

My guess is that `skip_until` is searching for a position or token at or after end-of-input. With no final newline that position is never reached, and the loop doesn't stop when the input runs out.

### Expected behavior

`format-nth` returns the formatted block (adding the final newline, as it does now when one is present), or returns an error. It should never spin forever.

### Workaround

Make sure files end with a newline (for example, VS Code `"files.insertFinalNewline": true`), or update snapshots with `moon test --update` from the terminal instead of the code lens.

### Environment

- moon 0.1.20261111 (8b8d15b 2026-11-11), with the moon-lsp bundled in `~/.moon/bin`
- moonc v0.10.21+cfd6c5d6c (2026-11-12)
- VS Code extension `moonbit.moonbit-lang` 0.7.2026111201
- macOS 27.2.1, arm64

title: wasm (linear memory): every bounds-checked array read calls two out-of-line helpers, about 3x slower than unsafe_get
body:
## Summary

In `--target wasm --release` output, each checked `FixedArray` read becomes two function calls: one that loads the array length from the header, and one that checks the index and traps. Neither is inlined, and the length is reloaded on every read even when it is loop-invariant. A loop that reads a table per input byte runs about 3 times as long as the same loop with `unsafe_get`. On wasm-gc and native the two versions run at the same speed.

## Repro

```moonbit
fn checked(table : FixedArray[Int], data : FixedArray[Byte]) -> Int {
  let mut sum = 0
  for i in 0..<data.length() {
    sum = sum + table[data[i].to_int()]
  }
  sum
}

fn unchecked(table : FixedArray[Int], data : FixedArray[Byte]) -> Int {
  let mut sum = 0
  for i in 0..<data.length() {
    sum = sum + table.unsafe_get(data.unsafe_get(i).to_int())
  }
  sum
}
```

Benchmarked with `moon bench --release` over 1 MiB of input (256-entry table), pinned to one core:

| target | checked | unchecked |
|---|---:|---:|
| wasm | 2.20 ms | 0.71 ms |
| wasm-gc | 0.68 ms | 0.68 ms |
| native | 0.38 ms | 0.38 ms |

## Generated code

The loop body of `checked` in the release `.wasm` (`wasm-tools print`), for one of the two reads:

```wat
local.get 12
i32.const 0
local.get 11
call 17        ;; length
i32.const 1
i32.sub
call 22        ;; range check
local.get 11
local.get 12
i32.add
i32.load8_u
```

with

```wat
(func (;17;) (param i32) (result i32)
  local.get 0
  i32.const 4
  i32.sub
  i32.load align=1)

(func (;22;) (param i32 i32 i32)
  local.get 0
  local.get 2
  i32.le_s
  if
    local.get 0
    local.get 1
    i32.ge_s
    if
    else
      unreachable
    end
  else
    unreachable
  end)
```

`unchecked` compiles to the bare `i32.load8_u` / `i32.load`.

## Expected

The length load and the check inlined at the access, ideally as one unsigned comparison (`index <u length`) and a trap, with the length hoisted when the array does not change in the loop. The effect is not limited to this example: a slice-by-8 CRC-32 runs 2.35 times as fast on wasm with its table reads unchecked, against 1.43 on wasm-gc and 1.13 on native.

## Environment

moonc v0.10.20+65efd5b93 (2026-11-05), moon 0.1.20261104, moonrun 0.1.20261104; Linux x86-64 (Intel Core i5-10400F).

title: `moon fmt`: interpolation-heavy string costs ~9.5x more per doubling (1.6 s -> 15 s)
body:
### Description

Formatting one function whose string literal contains `k` interpolation
segments (`\{i}`) grows much faster than the input:

| k | bytes | moonfmt wall time | peak RSS |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1024 | 6.6 KB | 1.56–1.61 s | ~21 MB |
| 2048 | 13.2 KB | 14.8–15.3 s | ~23 MB |

That is about 9.5x for 2x input. A plain string of the same byte size formats
in about 7 ms, so the cost tracks the number of segments rather than the input
size.

Expected: roughly linear in the number of segments. At minimum, 13 KB of input
should not take 15 s to format.

### Code

- Target: irrelevant

```bash
gen() {
  printf 'fn f() -> String { "'
  for ((i = 0; i < $1; i++)); do printf '\\{%d}' "$i"; done
  printf '" }\n'
}

gen 2048 > p.mbt
wc -c p.mbt
/usr/bin/time -f '%e s %M KB' moonfmt p.mbt -o out.mbt
```

### Environment

- moonfmt / moonc: v0.10.20+65efd5b93 (2026-11-05)
- OS: Linux x86_64, Ubuntu 24.04
- 3 runs per size; medians 1.60 s and 15.08 s

### Error output

None; the formatter exits 0 and the output is correct.

### Notes

Two sessions gave 1.576/15.072 s and 1.60/15.08 s medians. Two sizes are not
enough to identify a complexity class, so this report only claims the measured
inputs and the plain-string control, not an asymptotic order.

Reproducer: <https://github.com/I3eg1nner/moonc-fuzz/tree/main/poc/p1_fmt_interp>.

title: `moon fmt` prints unary plus as `~+`, producing code that cannot be re-parsed
body:
### Description

`moonc syncheck` accepts unary `+`:

```moonbit
fn f(y : Int) -> Int { +y }
fn main { println(f(1).to_string()) }
```

Typing then reports the internal name (`[4021] The value identifier ~+ is
unbound`), and `moonfmt` writes it back as `~+(y)`. Re-parsing the formatted
file fails:

```
[E3001] Lexing error: unrecognized character "~" (U+007E)
```

So `moon fmt` turns a file it can parse into a file it cannot parse. The same
happens for `+(1)`, `+(y)`, `x ++ y` and `x + ++y`; `+1` folds to `1`, and
unary-minus controls (`-y`, `-(y)`, `-1`, `x + -y`) are unaffected.

Expected: keep `+y` in the output (if unary plus is meant to be supported), or
reject it at parse time with a normal diagnostic. The formatter should not
emit a token the lexer rejects either way.

### Code

- Target: irrelevant

`u.mbt`:

```moonbit
fn f(y : Int) -> Int { +y }
fn main { println(f(1).to_string()) }
```

```bash
moonc syncheck u.mbt          # rc 0
moon check u.mbt              # rc 1, 4021 ~+ unbound
moonfmt u.mbt -o u1.mbt       # rc 0
moonc syncheck u1.mbt         # rc 2, E3001

cat u1.mbt
# fn f(y : Int32) -> Int32 {
#   ~+(y)
# }
```

`moonfmt` also rewrites `Int` to `Int32` in this standalone mode; that part is
expected and unrelated.

### Environment

- moonc / moonfmt: v0.10.20+65efd5b93 (2026-11-05)
- moon: 0.1.20261104 (940aa18 2026-11-04)
- OS: Linux x86_64, Ubuntu 24.04
- 5/5 reproductions

### Error output

```
u1.mbt:3:3-3:4 [E3001] Lexing error: unrecognized character "~" (U+007E)
```

### Notes

This is a syntax round-trip defect, not a semantic one: the original file
parses, so the claim is limited to the formatter/printer path. A larger matrix
of parse-accepted mutants shows the same signature, but this report only
depends on the committed sample.

Reproducer: <https://github.com/I3eg1nner/moonc-fuzz/tree/main/poc/f5_prefix_plus>.

title: ICE: native link rejects an exported closure-containing type with an ICE instead of a diagnostic
body:
### Description

A 10-line package fails at native link with an internal compiler error:

```
Error: Machine_error(kind=unsupported;
  who="Machine_of_clam_lower.reject_export_type_containing_unsupported_callback";
  message="the Native backend cannot export types containing closures")
```

The package declares `pkgtype(kind: "foreign_library")` and exports one
function with `#export_name`. Its parameter type is a struct with a private
closure field. Removing `#export_name` makes the same package build (rc 0), so
the trigger is exporting a type that reaches a closure, not the struct itself.

Expected: a normal "unsupported for native export" diagnostic with a source
location. An ICE with a mangled internal name is not actionable from a user
package.

This is a diagnostic/tooling defect, not a miscompile: the package's `.core`
is produced, the JS target is unaffected, and the same module builds once the
export attribute is removed.

### Code

- Target: native (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu)

`moon.mod`:

```
name = "f6min"
version = "0.1.0"
```

`moon.pkg`:

```
pkgtype(kind: "foreign_library")
```

`main.mbt`:

```moonbit
pub struct Handle {
  priv f : (Int32) -> Int32
}

#export_name("f6min_next")
pub fn next(h : Handle) -> Unit {
  ignore(h)
}
```

```bash
moon build --target native
echo $?      # 255
```

### Environment

- moonc: v0.10.20+65efd5b93 (2026-11-05)
- moon: 0.1.20261104 (940aa18 2026-11-04)
- OS: Linux x86_64, Ubuntu 24.04
- 3/3 reproductions

### Error output

```
Oops, the compiler has encountered an unexpected situation.
...
Error: Machine_error(kind=unsupported; who="Machine_of_clam_lower.reject_export_type_containing_unsupported_callback"; message="the Native backend cannot export types containing closures")
```

The failure happens in `moonc link-core`, i.e. after the package's own compile
step.

### Notes

Controls, all on the same file: no `#export_name` → rc 0; plain `pub fn`
instead of an exported one → rc 0. An external 12 MB package
(`WeiR-h/moonldif@0.7.6`) hits the same signature through `moon test --target
native`, while a `src`-scoped native build of that package succeeds; that
larger case is available in the reproducer directory but is not needed here.

Reproducer: <https://github.com/I3eg1nner/moonc-fuzz/tree/main/poc/f6_native_export_closure_min>.

title: ICE: SIGSEGV in `moonc syncheck` on a malformed `moon.pkg`
body:
### Description

`moonc syncheck moon.pkg` segfaults with no output (rc 139) on a 101-byte
ASCII file. The trigger depends on the token count and on the file not ending
with a newline:

| input | result |
|---|---|
| `s(` + 49 literals, no trailing newline | rc 2, parse errors |
| `s(` + 50 literals, no trailing newline (101 B) | SIGSEGV |
| `s(` + 50 literals, trailing newline | rc 2 |
| `s(` + 50 identifiers instead of number literals | rc 2 |

The same file used as a package manifest through the `moon` driver does not
crash: `moon build` reports a normal parse error (rc 255). The crash is on the
explicit `moonc syncheck` path.

### Code

- Target: irrelevant

```bash
printf 's(' > moon.pkg
printf '1,%.0s' $(seq 49) >> moon.pkg
printf '1' >> moon.pkg
wc -c moon.pkg        # 101
moonc syncheck moon.pkg
echo $?               # 139
```

gdb backtrace (no symbols beyond `camlMoonc*`):

```
#0 camlMoonc__next_segment_head_71310
#1 camlMoonc__report_failed_to_parse_71498
#2 camlMoonc__loop_71725
#3 camlMoonc__fun_428987
#4 camlMoonc__surround_71668
#5 camlMoonc__fun_429097
#6 camlMoonc__parse_apply_72880
#7 camlMoonc__parse_statement_72979
#8 camlMoonc__loop_71725
#9 camlMoonc__parse_statements_72989
#10 camlMoonc__moon_pkg_of_tokens_72993
#11 camlMoonc__parse_from_string_inner_429709
```

A second input, found independently by mutation (672 B: a truncated
`import { ... } for "wbtest"` block followed by an unterminated
`options(... targets: { ... })` map), hits the same top frames. Dropping the
last map entry turns it into a clean rc 2.

### Environment

- moonc: v0.10.20+65efd5b93 (2026-11-05)
- moon: 0.1.20261104 (940aa18 2026-11-04)
- OS: Linux x86_64, Ubuntu 24.04
- 3/3 reproductions for both inputs

### Error output

No stderr; the process dies with SIGSEGV and rc 139.

### Notes

This is a memory-safety bug in the parse-error path, but I have not proven the
root cause: the public 2025-03 source snapshot does not correspond to this
binary, so the crash site is known only from symbols and frames.

Reproducers and boundary experiments:
<https://github.com/I3eg1nner/moonc-fuzz/tree/main/poc/f1_moon_pkg_segv> and
<https://github.com/I3eg1nner/moonc-fuzz/tree/main/poc/f1b_pkg_map_segv>.

title: ICE: 19-byte parser input grows past 5 GiB and aborts (`moonc syncheck`)
body:
### Description

`moonc syncheck` on a 19-byte file aborts with `Fatal error: out of memory`.
With `RLIMIT_AS` set to 6 GiB it reaches 5.66 GiB peak RSS after 15.3 s and
dies with SIGABRT (rc 134). Without a cap, an earlier run reached 8.2 GiB in
20 s and was still growing; that control was not repeated.

The input is 19 bytes, so memory use is not bounded by input size. Any caller
that runs `syncheck` on untrusted input inherits the exhaustion.

Expected: an ordinary parse error (rc 2) with bounded memory.

### Code

- Target: irrelevant

```bash
printf 'fn r(){y(for in ]\n[' > main.mbt
wc -c main.mbt      # 19

# Do not run uncapped on a shared machine.
prlimit --as=6442450944 -- moonc syncheck main.mbt
echo $?             # 134
```

### Environment

- moonc: v0.10.20+65efd5b93 (2026-11-05)
- OS: Linux x86_64, Ubuntu 24.04
- 2/2 capped runs in the latest session; 5/5 in an earlier capped series

### Error output

```
Fatal error: out of memory
```

Process terminated by SIGABRT (rc 134). `/usr/bin/time` reports
`15.33 s`, `MAXRSS=5660616 KB`.

### Notes

The growth rate and whether the process terminates without a cap are not
characterized, so this report only claims that the capped run exhausts the
cap. The 19-byte input is reproduced verbatim above; no trailing newline after
`[`.

Reproducer: <https://github.com/I3eg1nner/moonc-fuzz/tree/main/poc/f3_parser_oom>.

title: ICE: invalid escape in a string literal reaches the typer as Invalid_argument("Char.chr")
body:
### Description

A string literal containing a backslash followed by a non-ASCII character is
accepted by the parser and then crashes the next stage:

```moonbit
let s = "\中"
fn main { println(s) }
```

`moonc syncheck main.mbt` returns 0, but `moonc build-package` aborts with
`Invalid_argument("Char.chr")`. A backslash followed by U+200B (zero-width
space) shows the same split: syncheck rc 0, build-package rc 199.

Expected: a lexer diagnostic for the invalid escape, at the stage that reads
the literal, instead of acceptance followed by an ICE.

### Code

- Target: wasm (also reproduces through `moon check`)

`main.mbt` (`\中` is backslash followed by U+4E2D):

```moonbit
let s = "\中"
fn main { println(s) }
```

```bash
moonc syncheck main.mbt
# rc 0, prints {"toplevel":{"fn":1,"let":1},"max-toplevel-span":"1-1"}

moonc build-package main.mbt -o main.core -pkg f2/p -pkg-type executable \
  -i "$HOME/.moon/lib/core/_build/wasm/release/bundle/builtin/builtin.mi:moonbitlang/core/builtin" \
  -i "$HOME/.moon/lib/core/_build/wasm/release/bundle/prelude/prelude.mi:prelude" \
  -pkg-sources f2/p:. -target wasm -g -O0 -workspace-path .
# rc 199, ICE
```

A package containing the same file also ICEs through `moon check` (driver
rc 1), so this is not specific to invoking `moonc` directly.

### Environment

- moonc: v0.10.20+65efd5b93 (2026-11-05)
- moon: 0.1.20261104 (940aa18 2026-11-04)
- OS: Linux x86_64, Ubuntu 24.04
- 3/3 reproductions (both witnesses)

### Error output

```
Oops, the compiler has encountered an unexpected situation.
This is a bug in the compiler.
...
Error: Invalid_argument("Char.chr")
```

### Notes

The second witness is `fn main { let s = "\<U+200B>" }`; its file is 27 bytes,
with `5c e2 80 8b` after the opening quote. It reaches `build-package` without
the `moon` driver, which is why it is included here.

The ICE message does not say where the exception is raised, and the public
2025-03 source snapshot does not match this binary, so this report does not
claim a specific root cause.

Reproducers: <https://github.com/I3eg1nner/moonc-fuzz/tree/main/poc/f2_lex_escape_ice>
and <https://github.com/I3eg1nner/moonc-fuzz/tree/main/poc/f2b_zwsp_escape_t2_ice>.

title: ICE: invalid UTF-8 in a `.mbt.md` file reaches Basic_utf8_decode.MalFormed
body:
### Description

A `.mbt.md` file whose MoonBit code fence contains raw invalid UTF-8 bytes
crashes `moonc syncheck` with `Moonc.Basic_utf8_decode.MalFormed` (rc 199).
The same file also crashes `moonc build-package`.

The `.mbt` path does not crash on this toolchain: a source file containing
`de ad be ef` returns the normal diagnostic `3001 Could not read the file
because it contains invalid UTF-8 streams`. So the decoder failure is specific
to the `.mbt.md` path.

This is related to #861, which reported `Moonc.Basic_utf8.MalFormed` for
`.mbt` files on v0.6.18. On v0.10.20 the `.mbt` path is clean and the exception
module has been renamed, but `.mbt.md` still reaches the decoder.

Expected: the same 3001 diagnostic, or any normal input error, instead of an
ICE.

### Code

- Target: irrelevant

`doc.mbt.md` is 40 bytes. Hexdump:

```
00000000: 2320 740a 0a60 6060 6d62 740a 666e 2066  # t..```mbt.fn f
00000010: 2829 207b 206c 6574 2073 203d 2022 fffe  () { let s = "..
00000020: 2220 7d0a 6060 600a                      " }.```.
```

Generate it and run:

```bash
printf '# t\n\n```mbt\nfn f() { let s = "' > doc.mbt.md
printf '\xff\xfe' >> doc.mbt.md
printf '" }\n```\n' >> doc.mbt.md
wc -c doc.mbt.md      # 40

moonc syncheck doc.mbt.md
echo $?               # 199
```

### Environment

- moonc: v0.10.20+65efd5b93 (2026-11-05)
- OS: Linux x86_64, Ubuntu 24.04
- 3/3 reproductions

### Error output

```
Oops, the compiler has encountered an unexpected situation.
This is a bug in the compiler.
...
Error: Moonc.Basic_utf8_decode.MalFormed
```

### Notes

A second witness, found by byte-level mutation, is a 6.7 KB `.mbt.md` with
invalid bytes at offset 6140; it produces the same exception class. It is kept
as a separate file because it replays without any generator script.

Reproducers: <https://github.com/I3eg1nner/moonc-fuzz/tree/main/poc/f4_invalid_utf8>
and <https://github.com/I3eg1nner/moonc-fuzz/tree/main/poc/f4b_invalid_utf8_2>.

title: moonc prove: parentheses around `||` inside `&&` are dropped in generated WhyML
body:
## Summary

When a logic-side predicate contains a parenthesized `||` under `&&`, `moonc prove` drops the parentheses in the generated WhyML. Since `/\` binds tighter than `\/` in Why3, `a && (b || c)` becomes `(a /\ b) \/ c`. The result is a silently weaker (or different) predicate, so a false postcondition can be reported as proved.

## Reproduction

```moonbit
// moon.pkg
proof_enabled = true
```

```moonbit
// p.mbtp
///|
predicate p(a : Bool, b : Bool, c : Bool) {
  a && (b || c)
}
```

```moonbit
// p.mbt
///|
/// `p(false, false, true)` is `false && (false || true)`, i.e. false,
/// so this postcondition should not be provable.
pub fn f(x : Int) -> Int where {
  proof_ensure: result => p(false, false, true),
} {
  x
}
```

Run `moon prove`.

## Expected

The goal fails, and the generated WhyML keeps the grouping:

```whyml
predicate p (a: bool) (b: bool) (c: bool) = a /\ (b \/ c)
```

## Actual

```
  Succeeded: 1 goals proved
Summary:
  1 of 1 packages proved
```

and `_build/verif/*.mlw` contains:

```whyml
predicate p (a: bool) (b: bool) (c: bool) = a /\ b \/ c
```

## Workaround

Move the inner disjunction into its own predicate, e.g. `a && q(b, c)` with `predicate q(b : Bool, c : Bool) { b || c }`.

## Environment

- OS: Linux, Debian 13 (trixie), aarch64
- moon 0.1.20261102 (ea07287 2026-11-02)
- moonc v0.10.19+bee578715 (2026-11-02)
- Why3 1.8.0, Z3 4.13.3

title: VS Code Test panel drops snapshot failure details (expected/actual diff and location)
body:
# VS Code Test panel drops snapshot failure details (expected/actual diff and location)

## Environment

- VS Code extension `moonbit.moonbit-lang` 0.7.2026103001
- moon 0.1.20261029 (ee2274c), moonc v0.10.19+97801ee1b
- VS Code 1.144.0, macOS

## Reproduction

```moonbit
test "snapshot" {
  debug_inspect(1 + 1, content="3")
}
```

Run this test from the VS Code Test panel.

## What happens

The test is marked failed, but the only output is:

```
test JonathanMEdwards/locus/zz_probe_wbtest.mbt::snapshot failed
```

The failure message in the Test panel has the same text. Neither shows the
expected and actual values or the diff, and there's no link to the failing
`debug_inspect`.

Running `moon test` from the command line prints the full diff, so the
information is lost inside the extension.

## Cause

The extension runs `moon test … --test-failure-json`. For a snapshot failure,
the JSON already holds everything needed:

```json
{"package":"JonathanMEdwards/locus","filename":"zz_probe_wbtest.mbt","index":"0","test_name":"snapshot","message":"@EXPECT_FAILED {\"loc\": {\"filename\":\"zz_probe_wbtest.mbt\",\"start_line\":2,\"start_column\":3,\"end_line\":2,\"end_column\":36}, \"args_loc\": [{\"filename\":\"zz_probe_wbtest.mbt\",\"start_line\":2,\"start_column\":17,\"end_line\":2,\"end_column\":22}, {\"filename\":\"zz_probe_wbtest.mbt\",\"start_line\":2,\"start_column\":32,\"end_line\":2,\"end_column\":35}, null, null], \"expect\": \"3\", \"actual\": \"2\" }"}
```

The function that formats the result throws that message away. From the
bundled `node/extension.js`:

```js
function NP(t){let e;return t.message.startsWith("@EXPECT_FAILED")||t.message.startsWith("@SNAPSHOT_TESTING")?e="":e=`: ${t.message}`,`test ${t.package}/${t.filename}::${t.test_name} failed${e}`}
```

`markTest` then passes the same string to `new TestMessage(...)`, so the Test
panel never receives the location or the expected and actual values.

## Suggested fix

For `@EXPECT_FAILED` messages, parse the JSON after the prefix and report the
failure with VS Code's diff message and its location:

```ts
const detail = JSON.parse(message.slice("@EXPECT_FAILED ".length));
const msg = vscode.TestMessage.diff(
  `${testName}: snapshot differs`,
  detail.expect,
  detail.actual,
);
msg.location = new vscode.Location(
  vscode.Uri.file(path.join(packageDir, detail.loc.filename)),
  new vscode.Range(
    detail.loc.start_line - 1, detail.loc.start_column - 1,
    detail.loc.end_line - 1, detail.loc.end_column - 1,
  ),
);
run.failed(testItem, msg);
```

VS Code then shows the failure inline at the `debug_inspect` call, with a
side-by-side diff in the test results view. `@SNAPSHOT_TESTING` messages
probably need the same treatment. For other failures, the text after
`failed: ` in the message could at least be shown, and its location parsed
where present.

## Expected

The Test panel shows each failure's message. For snapshot and `inspect`
failures it also shows the expected/actual diff, located at the failing
call, as the command-line `moon test` does in text.

title: JS source map: two source lines mapped to the same generated position, so breakpoints can't be set on the call's line
body:
# JS source map: two source lines mapped to the same generated position, so breakpoints can't be set on the call's line

## Environment

- moon 0.1.20261028 (e1e1f15), moonc v0.10.18+6c83a7f62 (2026-10-28)
- `--target js`, debug build (`-g -O0 -source-map`)
- macOS, Node v24.16.0, VS Code JavaScript debugger

## Reproduction

`moon.mod`:

```
name = "repro/smrepro"

version = "0.1.0"
```

`moon.pkg`: empty

`lib.mbt`:

```moonbit
///|
fn f(x : Int) -> Int raise {
  if x < 0 {
    fail("negative")
  }
  x + 1
}
```

`lib_wbtest.mbt`:

```moonbit
test {
  println("a")
  inspect(
    f(1), content="2")
}
```

Build with `moon test --target js -g --build-only`, then decode
`_build/js/debug/test/smrepro.whitebox_test.js.map`.

## What happens

The generated code for lines 3–4 evaluates `f(1)` first, then calls
`inspect`:

```js
const _bind$3 = _M0FP25repro7smrepro1f(1);           // mapped to line 4
if (_bind$3.$tag === 1) { ... } else { return _bind$3; }  // line 4
return _M0FPB15inspect_2einner({ self: _tmp, ... });  // line 3 AND line 4
```

The source map has two segments for the same generated position, the start
of the `return _M0FPB15inspect_2einner(...)` line, column 0. One maps to
`lib_wbtest.mbt` line 3 and the other to line 4.

## Effect

In VS Code, a breakpoint on line 3 (`inspect(`) cannot be set. The debugger
resolves line 3 to that generated position, maps it back, gets line 4, and
moves or rejects the breakpoint. Line 2 and line 4 accept breakpoints
normally.

This affects any call whose arguments are on a later line than the call
itself and include a call that can raise, a layout `moon fmt` produces often.

## Expected

Each generated position maps to one source location. Here, the start of the
`return inspect(...)` line should map only to line 3, so a breakpoint on
line 3 stops just before `inspect` is called.

Without `raise` on `f`, the call to `f` is inlined into the `inspect` line,
and line 3 maps correctly.

title: ICE: native debug 'aggregate stub wrapper arguments are not lowered' for extern "C" taking V128
body:
A native **debug** test build (`-g -O0`) fails to link when MoonBit code calls an `extern "C"` function that takes a `V128` argument. The error comes from the stub-wrapper lowering. `--release` builds the same code and the test passes.

We hit it in UsaGui (via lite-space's native `pod_store_v128(address : UInt64, value : V128)`). Until now it was hidden behind #1343: each link stops at its first machine error. It happens on moonc v0.10.15+943464bfa and v0.10.18+6c83a7f62. The reduction below is standalone.

### Code

- Target: native/c (Windows x86_64, MSVC), debug only

`moon.mod`:
```
name = "repro/v128stub"
```
`moon.pkg`:
```
import {
  "moonbitlang/core/v128",
}

options(
  "native-stub": [ "stub.c" ],
  targets: { "lib.mbt": [ "native" ] },
)
```
`stub.c`:
```c
#include "moonbit.h"
#include <stdint.h>
#include <string.h>
static unsigned char sink[16];
void repro_store_v128(uint64_t address, moonbit_v128_t value) { (void)address; memcpy(sink, &value, 16); }
```
`lib.mbt`:
```moonbit
///|
extern "C" fn store_v128(address : UInt64, value : V128) -> Unit = "repro_store_v128"

///|
pub fn store(x : Float) -> Unit {
  store_v128(0UL, @v128.f32x4_const(x, x, x, x))
}
```
`lib_test.mbt`:
```moonbit
///|
test "store" {
  store(1.0)
}
```

```
$ moon test --target native
Error: Machine_error(kind=unsupported; who="Machine_of_clam_lower.finish_stub_wrapper_shell"; message="aggregate stub wrapper arguments are not lowered in this batch")

Compiler args: "...moonc.exe" link-core ... -test-mode -target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc -g -O0

$ moon test --target native --release
Total tests: 1, passed: 1, failed: 0.
```

### Expected
The debug build links and the test passes, as in release.

### Workaround
Split the vector before the C call: `store_u64x2(address, @v128.i64x2_extract_lane(v, 0), @v128.i64x2_extract_lane(v, 1))`, with a C stub taking two `uint64_t`. This builds in both modes.

Related: #1343 (also a native debug `-O0` machine error, about calls with 13+ `#valtype` arguments).

title: ICE: native debug regalloc 'requires more GPR patch scratch registers' when a call passes 13+ #valtype arguments
body:
A call that passes 13 or more `#valtype` struct arguments fails to link in a native **debug** test build (`-g -O0`) with an internal error in the register allocator. 12 arguments work, a plain (non-`#valtype`) struct with the same fields works, and `--release` works.

We hit it in real code at three places (UsaGui `FrameKit::new` and `UiFrame::from_pod_regions`, which pass up to 19 `#valtype` `PodRegion { address : UInt64, byte_length : Int }` values, and a fuzz test), on moonc v0.10.15 and v0.10.18. The reduction below is standalone.

### Code

- Target: native/c (Windows x86_64, MSVC), debug only

`moon.mod`:
```
name = "repro/regalloc"
version = "0.1.0"
```
`moon.pkg`: empty.

`lib.mbt`:
```moonbit
///|
#valtype
pub(all) struct Region {
  address : UInt64
  byte_length : Int
}

///|
pub fn total(
  x0 : Region, x1 : Region, x2 : Region, x3 : Region, x4 : Region,
  x5 : Region, x6 : Region, x7 : Region, x8 : Region, x9 : Region,
  x10 : Region, x11 : Region, x12 : Region,
) -> Int {
  x0.byte_length + x1.byte_length + x2.byte_length + x3.byte_length +
  x4.byte_length + x5.byte_length + x6.byte_length + x7.byte_length +
  x8.byte_length + x9.byte_length + x10.byte_length + x11.byte_length +
  x12.byte_length
}

///|
pub fn run(rs : Array[Region]) -> Int {
  total(rs[0], rs[1], rs[2], rs[3], rs[4], rs[5], rs[6], rs[7], rs[8], rs[9], rs[10], rs[11], rs[12])
}
```

`lib_test.mbt`:
```moonbit
///|
test "thirteen valtype arguments" {
  let rs = Array::makei(13, i => ({ address: i.to_uint64(), byte_length: i } : Region))
  assert_eq(run(rs), 78)
}
```

```
$ moon test --target native
Error: Machine_error(kind=internal; who="Machine_regalloc_scan.patch_scratch_reg"; message="SSA scan instruction requires more GPR patch scratch registers than the target provides"; function="@_M0FP25repro8regalloc3run")

Compiler args: "...moonc.exe" link-core ... -test-mode -target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc -g -O0

$ moon test --target native --release
Total tests: 1, passed: 1, failed: 0.
```

| arguments | `#valtype` | result (debug) |
|---|---|---|
| 4, 6, 8, 12 | yes | pass |
| 13, 14, 15, 16 | yes | ICE |
| 16 | no (plain struct) | pass |

Named/labelled arguments with defaults (the real code's shape) fail the same way.

### Environment

- moon 0.1.20261012 (748b63c), moonc v0.10.15+943464bfa (2026-10-12); also seen on moonc v0.10.18+6c83a7f62 (2026-10-28)
- Windows 11 x86_64, MSVC toolchain (found by moon)
- Workaround: build and test native with `--release`.

title: ICE: link-core assertion when an async function calls a `raise?` parameter after a suspension
body:
An async function that calls a parameter of type `(A) -> B raise?` after a suspension point makes `moonc link-core` fail with an assertion. `moon check` passes; the crash happens only when a program that calls the function is linked (here, `moon test`).

It happens on js, wasm and native, with the pinned `0.10.17+d971670cd` and with the current `latest` (`0.10.18+6c83a7f62`). I could not try the `dev` channel: its download returned HTTP 403.

These variants link and pass, so the trigger seems to be the combination of an `async` function, a suspension, and a call to the `raise?` parameter:

| Variant | Result |
| --- | --- |
| As below | ICE |
| Same function, the function itself is `raise` (`-> T? raise`) | ICE |
| No suspension (`()` in place of `@aio.pause()`) | Pass |
| Parameter `(Int) -> T? raise` instead of `raise?` | Pass |
| Parameter `(Int) -> T?` (no raise) | Pass |
| Synchronous function with `raise?` parameter and `raise?` result | Pass |

Workaround: wrap the parameter in a synchronous function of type `(Int) -> T? raise`, and call the wrapper from the async code.

### Code

- Target: wasm, js, native/c (all three async targets)

`moon.mod`:

```
name = "example/ice-repro"
version = "0.0.1"
import {
  "moonbitlang/async@0.22.5",
}
```

`repro/moon.pkg`:

```
import {
  "moonbitlang/async" @aio,
}

supported_targets = "wasm+js+native"
```

`repro/repro.mbt`:

```moonbit
///|
pub async fn[T] pick(items : Array[Int], select : (Int) -> T? raise?) -> T? {
  @aio.pause()
  for item in items {
    if select(item) is Some(t) {
      return Some(t)
    }
  }
  None
}
```

`repro/repro_test.mbt`:

```moonbit
///|
async test "repro" {
  assert_eq(@repro.pick([1, 2], x => if x == 2 { Some(x) } else { None }), Some(2))
}
```

Run `moon test --target js` (or `wasm`, `native`).

### Environment

- OS: macOS
- OS distribution and/or version: Darwin 25.6.0
- CPU Architecture: arm64

```
moon 0.1.20261023 (3778465 2026-10-23)
moonc v0.10.17+d971670cd (2026-10-23)
moonrun 0.1.20261023 (3778465 2026-10-23)
```

Also with:

```
moon 0.1.20261028 (e1e1f15 2026-10-28)
moonc v0.10.18+6c83a7f62 (2026-10-28)
moonrun 0.1.20261028 (e1e1f15 2026-10-28)
```

### Error output

```
Error: failed to link example/ice-repro/repro (js, blackbox test): .../moonc link-core ... -main example/ice-repro/repro_blackbox_test ... -target js -g -O0 -source-map
Oops, the compiler has encountered an unexpected situation.
This is a bug in the compiler.
Error: File "moonc.ml", line 121880, characters 29-35: Assertion failed
```

With `0.10.18+6c83a7f62`: `Error: File "moonc.ml", line 123776, characters 29-35: Assertion failed`.

title: Linux native link-core stack overflow in MoonPlot ticker tests on stable and nightly
body:
MoonPlot's current-toolchain compatibility PR reproduces a compiler internal stack overflow on GitHub Ubuntu runners for native test linking. This is a compiler failure before test execution, not a failing runtime assertion.

Reproducer: clone https://github.com/moonbit-community/moonplot, checkout `38ed2c954490ef6d4cf823508257741474a478c2`, then run `MOON_WORK=off moon update` and `MOON_WORK=off moon test --target all --deny-warn`. The failing native packages are `Lampese/mathplotlib/ticker` (whitebox and blackbox) and `Lampese/mathplotlib/ticker/date` (blackbox). A narrower command to investigate is `MOON_WORK=off moon test ticker --target native --deny-warn`; this narrower form has not yet been independently reproduced on Linux.

Stable `moonc v0.10.18+6c83a7f62` job: https://github.com/moonbit-community/moonplot/actions/runs/40817330126/job/123261370889
Nightly `moonc v0.10.17+5802d87ac-nightly` job: https://github.com/moonbit-community/moonplot/actions/runs/40817330126/job/123261371077

Both logs report `moonc link-core ... -target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu -g -O0`, `Oops, the compiler has encountered an unexpected situation`, and `Error: Stack overflow`. Strict all-target checking succeeds first.

On local macOS, the same source and stable compiler pass complete debug and release suites: Wasm/Wasm-GC 22,678 tests each, JavaScript 22,740, native 22,682. The CI stack limit has not been increased and no test fixtures were removed. This is not a reduced reproducer; the complete exact source and logs above are available. Historical issue #784 concerned an older C backend overflow and is closed; this report records the current LLVM/Linux occurrence.

Consumer repair and release gate: https://github.com/moonbit-community/moonplot/pull/1 and https://github.com/moonbit-community/moonplot/issues/2.

title: Native runtime: moonbit_make_ref_valtype_array_raw under-allocates by 4 bytes on 32-bit targets (heap overflow)
body:
### Summary

`moonbit_make_ref_valtype_array_raw` (runtime.c; used for arrays of value types that hold references, e.g. `Array[BytesView]`, `Array[&Trait]`) writes a 16-byte prefix before the elements on every target, but sizes the allocation with `sizeof(void *)` for the extra header word. On 32-bit targets that is 4 bytes, so every such array writes 4 bytes past the end of its block.

Toolchain: moon 0.1.20261023 (3778465), moonc v0.10.17+d971670cd (2026-10-23); also 0.1.20261021 and 0.1.20261012.

### Code (`$MOON_HOME/lib/runtime/runtime.c`, lines 1516–1533 in this version)

```c
MOONBIT_EXPORT void *moonbit_make_ref_valtype_array_raw(int32_t len,
                                                        size_t valtype_size,
                                                        uint32_t layout_meta) {
  ...
  // the extra header is 4-byte but we allocate extra 8-byte for better
  // alignment
  size_t const total_size =
      len * valtype_size + sizeof(struct moonbit_object) + sizeof(void *);
  struct moonbit_object *obj = (struct moonbit_object *)MOONBIT_MALLOC_RAW(total_size);
  *(uint64_t *)obj = (uint64_t)layout_meta;                       // writes 8 bytes
  obj = (struct moonbit_object *)(((uint64_t *)obj) + 1);         // steps 8 bytes
  Moonbit_init_dynamic_rc(obj, moonbit_BLOCK_KIND_REF_VALTYPE_ARRAY);
  Moonbit_set_meta(obj, (uint32_t)len);
  return (void *)(obj + 1);                                       // elements at +16
}
```

The prefix is `struct moonbit_valtype_array_header` (the 8-byte `elem_header` + `padding`, then the 8-byte object header) = 16 bytes on every target. The allocation counts `sizeof(struct moonbit_object) + sizeof(void *)`: 8 + 8 = 16 on 64-bit hosts, but 8 + 4 = 12 on 32-bit targets, so the last 4 bytes of the elements lie outside the block.

### Minimal reproduction

Clean Ubuntu 22.04 x86-64 with `clang` (14.0.0) and `gcc-multilib` from apt and moon from the official installer; a 32-bit AddressSanitizer build, `MOON_CC=/path/to/cc32-asan moon build --target native --release cmd/main`.

`moon.mod`:
```
name = "repro/valtype"

version = "0.1.0"

preferred_target = "native"
```

`cmd/main/moon.pkg`:
```
pkgtype(kind: "executable")
```

`cmd/main/main.mbt`:
```moonbit
fn parts(data : Bytes) -> Array[BytesView] {
  [data[0:1], data[1:2], data[2:3]]
}

fn main {
  let a = parts(b"xyz")
  let mut n = 0
  for v in a {
    n += v.length()
  }
  println(n)
}
```

`cc32-asan`, the `MOON_CC` wrapper: everything 32-bit with ASan, the runtime with the system allocator, the 64-bit prebuilt runtime parts left out (an `ar` next to it: `ln -s /usr/bin/ar`):

```sh
#!/bin/bash
args=()
for a in "$@"; do
  case "$a" in
    -DMOONBIT_ALLOCATOR=MOONBIT_ALLOCATOR_MIMALLOC) args+=(-DMOONBIT_ALLOCATOR=MOONBIT_ALLOCATOR_SYSTEM) ;;
    -DMOONBIT_ALLOW_STACKTRACE | -DMOONBIT_USE_SIMDUTF | */libmoonbitrun.o | */libbacktrace.a) ;;  # 64-bit prebuilt parts
    *) args+=("$a") ;;
  esac
done
exec clang -m32 -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g "${args[@]}"
```

Output (`main.exe: ELF 32-bit LSB pie executable, Intel 80386`):

```
==92==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0xf6200f80 at pc 0x566e62de bp 0xffbec2b8 sp 0xffbec2b0
WRITE of size 4 at 0xf6200f80 thread T0
```

The default 64-bit build of the same program prints `3`. With only the allocation size changed as below, the 32-bit ASan build prints `3` too and ASan is silent (as are 32-bit ASan builds of our larger test suites).

title: Native runtime: moonbit_get_ms_since_epoch (`@env.now()`) wraps around on 32-bit targets
body:
### Summary

`$MOON_HOME/lib/runtime/env.c` (POSIX branch), used by `@env.now()` (`moonbitlang/core/env`, `env_native.mbt`: `extern "c" fn now_internal() -> UInt64 = "moonbit_get_ms_since_epoch"`):

```c
uint64_t moonbit_get_ms_since_epoch() {
  struct timeval tv;
  gettimeofday(&tv, 0);
  return tv.tv_sec * 1000 + tv.tv_usec / 1000;
}
```

`tv.tv_sec * 1000` is computed in the type of `tv_sec`. Where that is a 32-bit `long` (32-bit Linux without 64-bit `time_t`, e.g. i386; armhf with the default `time_t`), the product of today's seconds and 1000 overflows (signed overflow, undefined behaviour) before the conversion to `uint64_t`, so `@env.now()` returns a wrapped value. We noticed it as certificate validity checks failing (`BadCertificateTimeInvalid`) in a 32-bit build of a program that uses the wall clock.

Toolchain: moon 0.1.20261023 (3778465), moonc v0.10.17+d971670cd (2026-10-23); also 0.1.20261021.

### Minimal reproduction

Clean Ubuntu 22.04 x86-64 with `clang` (14.0.0) and `gcc-multilib` from apt and moon from the official installer; a 32-bit build, `MOON_CC=/path/to/cc32 moon build --target native --release cmd/main`.

`cc32`, the `MOON_CC` wrapper (an `ar` next to it: `ln -s /usr/bin/ar`):

```sh
#!/bin/bash
args=()
for a in "$@"; do
  case "$a" in
    -DMOONBIT_ALLOCATOR=MOONBIT_ALLOCATOR_MIMALLOC) args+=(-DMOONBIT_ALLOCATOR=MOONBIT_ALLOCATOR_SYSTEM) ;;
    -DMOONBIT_ALLOW_STACKTRACE | -DMOONBIT_USE_SIMDUTF | */libmoonbitrun.o | */libbacktrace.a) ;;  # 64-bit prebuilt parts
    *) args+=("$a") ;;
  esac
done
exec clang -m32 "${args[@]}"
```

`moon.mod`:
```
name = "repro/now"

version = "0.1.0"

preferred_target = "native"
```

`cmd/main/moon.pkg`:
```
import {
  "moonbitlang/core/env",
}

pkgtype(kind: "executable")
```

`cmd/main/main.mbt`:
```moonbit
fn main {
  println(@env.now())
}
```

Output (`main.exe: ELF 32-bit LSB pie executable, Intel 80386`), next to the host clock (`date +%s%3N`):

```
host clock: 1792787454148
1786091717
```

(1792787454148 mod 2^32 = 1786091716: the milliseconds were computed in 32 bits.)

title: ICE: Sys_error "No such file or directory" when building with --target llvm (std bundle dir is named `native`, not `llvm`)

-->

`moon build --target llvm` ICEs on **every** package, even an empty one. The
cause is a name mismatch between the target and the prebuilt standard-library
bundle shipped with the toolchain: the native bundle directory is named
`native`, but `moonc` is handed `-std-path ...\lib\core\_build\llvm\release\bundle`.

Evidence from the installed toolchain:

```
lib\core\_build\                                       -> [js, wasm, native, wasm-gc, ...]   (no "llvm")
lib\core\_build\native\release\bundle\prelude\prelude.mi   exists = true
lib\core\_build\native\release\bundle\abort\abort.mi       exists = true
lib\core\_build\llvm\release\bundle\prelude\prelude.mi     exists = false
lib\core\_build\llvm\release\bundle\abort\abort.mi         exists = false
```

`moonc` therefore fails to open the first `.mi` under `-std-path` and aborts
with an uncaught `Sys_error`, which is reported as an ICE.

### Reproducing steps

1. Any MoonBit project containing a `main.mbt` (the body does not matter).
2. Run `moon build --target llvm` (also reproduces with `moon check --target llvm`
   and `moon run --target llvm`).

### Expected behaviour

- `--target llvm` should resolve to `_build\native\release\bundle` (or the
  toolchain should also ship an `llvm` bundle directory / alias).
- If the std bundle for the requested target is not installed, emit a clear
  diagnostic such as *"std bundle for target `llvm` is not installed; use
  `--target native` or build core first"* instead of an ICE.

- Target: native/llvm

```moonbit
fn main {
  println("hello")

title: moonc folds x + 0.0 to x, which is wrong for x = -0.0 (IEEE 754 6.3), on every backend
body:
`moonbitlang/moonbit-compiler` has issues disabled, so I am reporting this here. The bug is in the compiler (a floating-point simplification), not in core's library code. cc @Yu-zh

## Summary

moonc rewrites `x + 0.0` to `x`. That is wrong for `x = -0.0`: IEEE 754-2019 §6.3 says `(-0) + (+0)` is `+0` in every rounding direction except `roundTowardNegative`, but the compiled program returns `-0`. It happens on wasm, wasm-gc, js and native, in debug and release. The same expression with a runtime zero is correct.

## Reproduction

`moon.mod`: any module. `src/moon.pkg`: `options("is-main": true)`.

```moonbit
fn main {
  let zero = @env.args().length() >> 30      // a runtime zero the optimizer cannot see
  let pz = 0.0 + zero.to_double()
  let nz = -pz                               // -0.0
  println((nz + pz).reinterpret_as_uint64().to_string(radix=16))   // 0                (correct)
  println((nz + 0.0).reinterpret_as_uint64().to_string(radix=16))  // 8000000000000000 (wrong, should be 0)
  println((nz - 0.0).reinterpret_as_uint64().to_string(radix=16))  // 8000000000000000 (correct: -0 - +0 = -0)
}
```

`moon run src --target <wasm|wasm-gc|js|native>` with and without `--release` prints the same three lines.

## What each backend does on its own

| Backend | Its own `(-0) + (+0)` | its own `(-0) - (+0)` | MoonBit `x + 0.0` for x = -0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| wasm, wasm-gc | `f64.add` gives `+0` | `f64.sub` gives `-0` | `-0` |
| js | `-0 + 0` gives `+0` | `-0 - 0` gives `-0` | `-0` |
| native (C, clang `-O0`/`-O2`/`-O3`) | `+0`, also with a literal `0.0` | `-0` | `-0` |

All three implementations follow IEEE 754 here (I checked a hand-built wasm module with only `f64.add`/`f64.sub` in Node, plain JavaScript in Node, and a small C program), so this is not a difference in backend semantics; the result is produced by the compiler's simplification `x + 0.0 -> x`. Folding `x - 0.0` to `x` is correct and is not the problem. clang does not fold `x + 0.0` at `-O3` either.

## Impact

Code that normalizes a negative zero with `+ 0.0` (a common idiom, for example in error-free transformations such as Fast2Sum) silently keeps `-0`. We found it because a randomized audit of `luna-utils` compared the result of `fast_two_sum` with an exact model.

## Environment

- moon 0.1.20261012 (748b63c 2026-10-12), moonc v0.10.15+943464bfa (2026-10-12)
- macOS arm64; wasm, wasm-gc and js run on Node v26.11.1

Found by [Luna-Flow/luna-utils#62](https://github.com/Luna-Flow/luna-utils/issues/62).

title: Native release: UInt taken from UInt? is treated as signed (to_uint64 sign-extends, >> is arithmetic)
Long paths (> 260 chars) passed from moon to moonc cause moonc ICE on Windows
body:
### Description

On Windows, when `moon` passes file paths longer than 260 characters to `moonc`, `moonc` hits an internal compiler error (ICE).

### Suggested fix

Consider using the `\\?\` prefix for long paths on Windows to lift the `MAX_PATH` limit when invoking `moonc`.

### How to reproduce

On SeekMoon (Windows), running `mbtx` with a dependency that includes `async` reliably triggers the issue.

title: ICE: native debug Array::push of #valtype record with enum fails in lower_array_make
body:
### Reproduction

Save this as `repro.mbt` and run `moon run repro.mbt --target native` (debug mode):

```moonbit
enum Kind {
  Ref(String)
}

#valtype
struct Entry {
  id : Int
  kind : Kind
}

fn main {
  let values : Array[Entry] = []
  values.push({ id: 0, kind: Kind::Ref("x") })
  println(values[0].id)
  match values[0].kind {
    Kind::Ref(x) => println(x)
  }
}
```

The source type-checks, but native debug linking fails in `moonc link-core`. The same file runs and prints `0` then `x` with `moon run repro.mbt --target native --release` and `moon run repro.mbt --target wasm-gc`. The `Array::push` path reaches an uninitialized array allocation for this `#valtype` record. I also reproduced the same diagnostic with an explicit `Array::unsafe_make_uninit` followed by initialization before reading.

Expected: native debug should compile and produce the same output as native release. If this type/operation is unsupported on native debug, a normal source diagnostic would be preferable to an internal compiler error.

### Environment

- Debian GNU/Linux 13 (trixie), x86_64
- `moon 0.1.20260920 (914d7da 2026-09-20)`
- `moonc v0.10.14+7d59c7ec9 (2026-09-18)`
- `moonrun 0.1.20260920 (914d7da 2026-09-20)`
- Feature flags: `rr_moon_mod,rr_moon_pkg`

### Native debug error

```text
Oops, the compiler has encountered an unexpected situation.
This is a bug in the compiler.
Error: Machine_error(kind=unsupported; who="Machine_of_clam_lower.lower_array_make"; message="uninitialized non-null GC ref arrays are not lowered"; function="@_M0MPB18UninitializedArray23unsafe__make__and__blitGRP34moon4test6single5EntryE")
moonc version: v0.10.14+7d59c7ec9
```

This reports an unsupported lowering path; the reproducer does not determine whether the language contract requires support for this particular representation.

title: ICE: Machine_of_clam_lower.lower_break: "break value is required for scalar loop"
body:
A value-less `break` inside a `while` loop crashes native codegen when the loop is
the last statement before the enclosing function's tail expression, and that tail
expression is an unboxed scalar literal / enum constructor (e.g. `0`, `true`,
`RankDir::TB`). The compiler classifies the loop as a value-producing "scalar loop"
and then raises a `type_mismatch` in `Machine_of_clam_lower.lower_break` because the
`break` carries no value.

Regression: the identical pattern compiled fine with earlier nightlies; this looks
like a recent regression in `Machine_of_clam_lower`.

### Code

- Target: native/llvm (`aarch64-apple-darwin`, `-g -O0`, test-mode)

```moonbit
pub fn mwe_walk() -> Int {
  while true {
    break
  }
  0
}

test "mwe walk reproduces scalar loop break ICE" {
  assert_eq(mwe_walk(), 0)
}
```

Reproduce with (single test block, not whole package):

```bash
moon test /path/to/mwe_test.mbt --index 0 --target native
```

Bisection notes (all variants below were reduced from the repro; every one
produces the same ICE, confirmed on `v0.10.11+8f8e8db1e`):

- `while true` is **not** required — a normal condition works:
  ```moonbit
  pub fn walk(start : Int) -> Int {
    let mut current = start
    while current >= 0 {
      if current < 0 { break }
      current = current - 1
    }
    0
  }
  ```
- Loop body can be a bare `break` (no `match`/`if`/`mut`) — the minimal repro above.
- Crashing tail expressions: `0` (Int literal), `true` (Bool literal), enum
  constructor (`MweRank::TB`).
- **Not** crashing tails: a variable (`let result = 0; ...; result`), a `String`
  literal (`"TB"`), or any statement between loop and tail (`...; let _ = current; 0`).
- Without a `break` in the loop, no crash.

Real-world trigger: in the Graphviz port, `graph_rankdir` ends with
`while true { ...; match p { Some(x) => current = x; None => break } }` immediately
followed by `RankDir::TB`.

### Environment

- OS: macOS
- OS distribution and/or version: macOS 26.6.2 (Build 25G83)
- CPU Architecture: arm64

title: ICE: Moonc.Hashed_type.Unresolved_type_variable on malformed lexmatch arms (string-literal patterns in tuple form)
body:
## Description

`moonc` crashes with an internal compiler error instead of reporting a syntax/type error when a `lexmatch` expression uses (invalid) plain string-literal patterns in tuple form across two arms, and a later arm's `as` binding is used in string interpolation.

```
Error: Moonc.Hashed_type.Unresolved_type_variable
```

## Minimal reproduction

```moonbit
fn f(s : String) -> String {
  lexmatch s {
    ("a", r) => ""
    ("b" as y, _) => "\{y}"
  }
}

fn main {  }
```

Run with:

```sh
moon run --target native -e '<the snippet above>'
```

The code is invalid on purpose — `lexmatch` arms should use `re"..."` literals (e.g. `(re"^a" as x, after=rest)`), so the expected outcome is an ordinary syntax error. With a **single** malformed arm the compiler does report normal errors (3002/4021); the ICE appears once there are **two** such arms and a later arm's `as`-bound variable is interpolated.

Nearby variants that do NOT crash (each reports ordinary errors):

- single arm: `("a" as x, r) => "\{x}"` only
- two arms whose bodies don't use the bindings: `=> ()` / `=> ""`
- two arms without `as`: `("a", r) / ("b", _)`

## Environment

- moonc: v0.10.8+8606a5800
- moon: 0.1.20260814 (a2de5b2 2026-08-14)
- OS: macOS (darwin arm64)
- backend: native (also reproduces the same way it was first hit, via `moon run -e`)

title: `#deprecated(skip_current_package=true)` still warns the package's own blackbox tests
body:
`#deprecated("…", skip_current_package=true)` suppresses the deprecation alert for callers **in the declaring package**. But a package's *blackbox* tests (`*_test.mbt` that reference the package as `@pkg`) compile as a separate `<pkg>_blackbox_test` package, so they still receive the alert.

Concretely: deprecating a promoted method such as `Hash::hash` with `skip_current_package=true` still flags the package's own test call sites (`x.hash()`), forcing them to migrate to `Hash::hash(x)`. In this migration that was ~130 call sites in the library's own tests — exactly the callers `skip_current_package` seems intended to spare.

### Repro

```moonbit
// pkg/foo.mbt
#deprecated("use bar instead", skip_current_package=true)
pub fn Foo::deprecated_thing(self : Foo) -> Unit { … }
```
```moonbit
// pkg/foo_test.mbt   (blackbox test)
test { @pkg.Foo::new().deprecated_thing() }   // deprecation alert fires here
```

### Ask

Treat a package's own black/white-box tests as "current package" for `skip_current_package` (they are the same codebase), or provide a flag that does.

### Environment

- `moon 0.1.20260713 (75c7e1f 2026-07-13)`
- `moonc v0.10.4+2cc641edf (2026-07-15)`
- macOS (arm64), `latest` channel
- Found while enabling `implicit_impl_as_method` in moonbitlang/core (PR #3846).

title: `#warnings("-implicit_impl_as_method")` is a no-op — no per-declaration suppression for E0079
body:
The `#warnings("…")` attribute documents per-declaration warning control, but `#warnings("-implicit_impl_as_method")` (and the numeric `#warnings("-79")`) placed on a top-level declaration has **no effect** — the E0079 warning still fires. Only the package-level `warnings = "-implicit_impl_as_method"` in `moon.pkg` suppresses it.

```moonbit
///|
#warnings("-implicit_impl_as_method")
pub impl Show for MyType with fn output(self, logger) { … }   // E0079 still reported on this line
```

The attribute docs do note *"this attribute only works with some specific warnings,"* so this may be intended — but per-declaration granularity is exactly the lever needed for the rare impls that genuinely can't be `extend`ed (e.g. a promotion of a **deprecated** trait method, where the `extend` would itself error), instead of disabling the warning for an entire package.

### Ask

Extend `#warnings` to cover `implicit_impl_as_method` (E0079), and ideally document precisely which warnings the attribute currently supports.

### Environment

- `moon 0.1.20260713 (75c7e1f 2026-07-13)`
- `moonc v0.10.4+2cc641edf (2026-07-15)`
- macOS (arm64), `latest` channel
- Found while enabling `implicit_impl_as_method` in moonbitlang/core (PR #3846).

title: `implicit_impl_as_method` (E0079): the suggested `pub extend` fix often doesn't compile (tuples → E4024, qualified path → E4020)
body:
The `implicit_impl_as_method` (E0079) warning suggests *"Add a `pub extend <Type> with <Trait>::{…}` declaration"*, but the suggested text frequently does not compile as written.

**Case 1 — tuple types (`[E4024]`).** For a tuple trait impl the message names the type `Tuple2`…`Tuple16`:

> Add a `pub extend Tuple10 with Compare::{op_lt, op_le, op_ge, compare, op_gt}` declaration …

But `Tuple10` is not a writable identifier:

```
[E4024] The type/trait Tuple10 is not found.
```

(A workaround exists — declare a transparent alias `pub type Tuple10[A, …] = (A, …)` and `extend` that — but the suggested fix as printed cannot be used.)

**Case 2 — fully-qualified trait path (`[E4020]`).** The message prints the canonical path, e.g. `@moonbitlang/core/debug.Debug::{to_repr}`. In a file that imports the package under its short alias you must rewrite the prefix by hand; in a file where the trait is only in scope **unqualified** (e.g. via the prelude in a blackbox test), the printed qualified form fails:

```
[E4020] Package "debug" not found in the loaded packages.
```

### Expected

The suggested `pub extend …` should be copy-pasteable: use the type/trait as spelled in the current file's scope, and either avoid suggesting `pub extend TupleN` for structural tuple types or support naming them directly.

### Repro

Enable `+implicit_impl_as_method` in `moon.mod` of `moonbitlang/core`; the tuple impls and `derive(@debug.Debug)` sites emit the unusable suggestions.

### Environment

- `moon 0.1.20260713 (75c7e1f 2026-07-13)`
- `moonc v0.10.4+2cc641edf (2026-07-15)`
- macOS (arm64), `latest` channel
- Found while enabling `implicit_impl_as_method` in moonbitlang/core (PR #3846).

title: ICE: Ctype.Unify when `extend`ing two trait methods that both conflict with existing regular methods
body:
While enabling the `implicit_impl_as_method` warning across `moonbitlang/core`, `moonc` ICEs with `Moonc.Ctype.Unify` when a `pub extend T with Trait::{m1, m2}` promotes **two** trait methods that both conflict with an already-defined regular method.

The key signal: extending **either method alone** reports a clean `[E4056]` ("method already defined"), but extending **both together** crashes the compiler.

### Code

- Target: all (reproduces on `moon check` default target and under `--target all`)

In a checkout of `moonbitlang/core` (reproduced at commit `51cf2bc3`), `StringBuilder::write_object` carries `#alias(write)` and `#alias(write_string_interpolation)` (`builtin/stringbuilder.mbt`), so both names already resolve to a regular method. Add a file `builtin/ice.mbt`:

```moonbit
///|
pub extend StringBuilder with Logger::{write, write_string_interpolation}
```

then `moon check`:

```
Oops, the compiler has encountered an unexpected situation.
This is a bug in the compiler.
Error: Moonc.Ctype.Unify
```

Contrast — the single-method form compiles to a proper diagnostic:

```moonbit
pub extend StringBuilder with Logger::{write_string_interpolation}   // => Error: [4056] method already defined
```

So the compiler handles one `extend`/method conflict correctly (E4056) but crashes when two are present in the same `extend`.

### Expected

A normal diagnostic (e.g. `[E4056]` per conflicting method), never an ICE.

### Environment

- `moon 0.1.20260713 (75c7e1f 2026-07-13)`
- `moonc v0.10.4+2cc641edf (2026-07-15)`
- macOS (arm64), `latest` channel
- Found while enabling `implicit_impl_as_method` in moonbitlang/core (PR #3846).

title: ICE: native test link fails when layout table exceeds 22-bit offset
body:
Running one existing native whitebox test in a public repository crashes during `moonc link-core`, before the test runs.

The test selection is intentionally narrow: changing the `-f` filter does not help because the native whitebox-test core for the package is still built and linked as one unit.

### Reproducing steps

```sh
git clone https://github.com/bit-vcs/bit.git
cd bit
git checkout 93b37e0cc956960d8db871ef803d94b63e66f506
moon test -p mizchi/bit/cmd/bit --target native \
  -f 'pack helpers: pack_hash_hex supports sha256 trailer'
```

The selected test is an existing, small test in [`pack_helpers_wbtest.mbt`](https://github.com/bit-vcs/bit/blob/93b37e0cc956960d8db871ef803d94b63e66f506/modules/bit/cmd/bit/pack_helpers_wbtest.mbt#L47-L51).

### Code

- Target: native

```moonbit
test "pack helpers: pack_hash_hex supports sha256 trailer" {
  let (pack, _) = make_sha256_ref_delta_pack_for_helpers()
  let expected = @bitcore.hash_prefix(pack, pack.length() - 32, hash_size=32)
  assert_eq(pack_hash_hex(pack, hash_size=32), expected.to_hex())
}
```

The test itself is not related to layouts. The package's generated native whitebox-test core is 31,323,407 bytes and is linked with 111 `.core` inputs. Using the one-test filter still reaches the same linker stage and fails.

I also tried standalone generated modules with:
- 30,000 functions returning `String`
- 1,000 distinct `String` record layouts (500,500 fields total)

Neither reproduced the ICE, so the command above is the smallest verified public reproducer I have so far.

### Environment

- OS: macOS
- OS distribution and/or version: macOS 26.5.2 (25F84)
- CPU Architecture: arm64

```
moon 0.1.20260713 (75c7e1f 2026-07-13) ~/.moon/bin/moon

Feature flags enabled: rr_moon_mod,rr_moon_pkg

### Error output

```
Error: Machine_error(
  kind=internal;
  who="Machine_runtime_header.add_layout";
  message="machine layout table exceeds 22-bit offset"
)
```

The failing invocation is `moonc link-core ... -target aarch64-apple-darwin -g -O0`.

title: Wasm backend miscompiles a #valtype struct with a Double first field returned from a raise function (i32.wrap_i64 expected i64, found f64)
body:
## Summary

On the **`wasm`** target, a `#valtype` struct whose **first field is a `Double`**, when returned from a **`raise`-capable** function, is miscompiled: `moonc` emits an `i32.wrap_i64` that consumes the struct's `f64` slot, producing invalid Wasm that fails validation at instantiation:

```
CompileError: WebAssembly.Module(): Compiling function "..._run" failed:
  i32.wrap_i64[0] expected type i64, found local.get of type f64
```

`native`, `wasm-gc`, and `js` all compile and run the same code correctly — it is **wasm-specific**.

## Minimal reproduction (self-contained, builtin types only)

`moon.mod.json`
```json
{ "name": "repro", "version": "0.1.0" }
```

`moon.pkg.json`
```json
{}
```

`top.mbt`
```moonbit
#valtype
priv struct W {
  value : Double
}

priv suberror E

fn make(i : Int64) -> W raise E {
  if i < 0L {
    raise E
  }
  { value: i.to_double() }
}

fn run(i : Int64) -> Double {
  match (try? make(i)) {
    Ok({ value }) => value
    Err(_) => -1.0
  }
}

test {
  ignore(run(123L))
}
```

Run:
```
moon test --target wasm
```

## Trigger conditions

All three are required:
1. the struct is annotated `#valtype`,
2. its **first field is a `Double`** (f64), and
3. it is produced by a function that can `raise` (the `Result`-of-struct lowering).

The struct's other fields are irrelevant — even a single `Double` field reproduces it, and a non-`Double` first field (any reference, `Option`, or plain `Int`) does not. It is not about reference/`Option` fields; in the original `@json` case the `StringView?` second field was incidental.

| variant | result |
|---|---|
| `{ value : Double }` (single Double field) | **FAIL** |
| `{ value : Double; other : Int }` (two scalars) | **FAIL** |
| `{ value : Double; repr : StringView? }` (Double first) | **FAIL** |
| `{ repr : StringView?; value : Double }` (Double **not** first) | PASS |
| `{ a : Int; value : Double }` (Int first) | PASS |
| remove `#valtype` (plain boxed struct) | PASS |
| remove `raise` / `try?` (no exceptions) | PASS |

Construction-and-return alone triggers it (no field read / destructure needed), as long as the producer is `raise`-capable.

## Workarounds

- order the fields so the first field is not a `Double`, or
- drop `#valtype`, or
- make the producer non-`raise`.

## Toolchain

```
moon 0.1.20260618 (afb4494 2026-06-18)
moonc v0.10.1+a46be2066 (2026-06-22)
moonrun 0.1.20260618 (afb4494 2026-06-18)
```

Found while replacing a `(Double, StringView?)` tuple with a `#valtype` struct in `@json` number lexing (moonbitlang/core#3639); the field-order workaround is in use there.

title: Primitive `Bytes == Bytes` in a contracted function generates invalid WhyML typing
Contracts over mutable wrapper functions reject mut-field reads and writes
body:
Moon version: `moon 0.1.20260608 (60bc8c3 2026-06-08)`

I made a minimal repro for contracts over a mutable wrapper function.

Minimal repro:
- Repo: https://github.com/mingyang91/fm-ledger-mbt/tree/54abd552d95bf09b3a5258845ac755dfab8ef155/repro_mbt_mut_world_contract
- Command:
  ```sh
  cd repro_mbt_mut_world_contract
  moon prove repro
  ```

The repro is intentionally tiny:

```moonbit
pub(all) struct Tables {
  balance : Int64
} derive(Eq, Debug)

pub(all) struct World {
  mut tables : Tables
}

pub fn deposit_tables(tables : Tables, amount : Int64) -> Tables where {
  proof_require: amount > 0L,
  proof_ensure: result => result.balance == tables.balance + amount,
} {
  { balance: tables.balance + amount }
}

pub fn deposit(world : World, amount : Int64) -> Int64 where {
  proof_require: amount > 0L,
  proof_ensure: result => result == amount,
  proof_ensure: result => world.tables.balance >= amount,
} {
  world.tables = deposit_tables(world.tables, amount)
  amount
}
```

Runtime-wise this shape is fine: a mutable `World` with a thin wrapper that mutates `world.tables` and returns only the business result.

Actual result from `moon prove repro`:
```text
Error: [4207]
  proof_ensure: result => world.tables.balance >= amount,
  unsupported expression in logic body

Error: [4207]
  world.tables = deposit_tables(world.tables, amount)
  unsupported expression in contracted function body
```

So the current impression is:
- pure transitions over immutable values prove fine
- but once a contract is placed on a mutating wrapper, the proof front-end rejects mutable-field reads/writes and post-state facts about that mutable field

Question:
- Is this current limitation expected?
- If yes, is the intended style to always keep proof contracts off mutating wrappers and only prove the pure inner transition?
- If not, is there a supported way to express post-state properties over a mutable field like `world.tables`?

title: Proof contracts reject lookup-based replay theorem shapes

  moon prove repro
  ```

The repro has a tiny `Table::lookup(id)` and a tiny transition `open_or_replay(table, id)`.

I would expect both of these theorem-style shapes to be expressible:

1. Direct lookup in `proof_require`
   ```moonbit
   fn replay_is_noop_direct(table : Table, id : Int64, existing : Row) -> Bool where {
     proof_require: table.lookup(id) == Some(existing),
     proof_ensure: result => result,
   } {
     let step = open_or_replay(table, id)
     step.ok && step.row == existing && step.patch.is_empty()
   }
   ```

2. Wrapped helper in `proof_require`
   ```moonbit
   fn lookup_matches_existing(table : Table, id : Int64, existing : Row) -> Bool where {
     proof_axiomatized: true,
     ...
   } {
     table.lookup(id) == Some(existing)
   }

   fn replay_is_noop_wrapped(...) -> Bool where {
     proof_require: lookup_matches_existing(table, id, existing),
     proof_ensure: result => result,
   } {
     let step = open_or_replay(table, id)
     step.ok && step.row == existing && step.patch.is_empty()
   }
   ```

Actual result:
- `proof_require: table.lookup(id) == Some(existing)` is rejected with
  `only direct logic-function calls, pure function calls, supported function-value applications, and primitive operators are supported in logic body`
- the wrapped helper in `proof_require` is also rejected with the same class of error
- the contracted body then rejects
  - `step.row == existing`
  - `step.patch.is_empty()`
  with `unsupported expression in contracted function body` / `unresolved method calls are not supported in contracted function bodies`

Excerpt:
```text
Error: [4207]
  proof_require: table.lookup(id) == Some(existing),
  only direct logic-function calls, pure function calls, supported function-value applications, and primitive operators are supported in logic body

Error: [4207]
  proof_require: lookup_matches_existing(table, id, existing),
  only direct logic-function calls, pure function calls, supported function-value applications, and primitive operators are supported in logic body

Error: [4207]
  step.ok && step.row == existing && step.patch.is_empty()
  unresolved method calls are not supported in contracted function bodies
```

Question:
- Is this current behavior expected?
- If yes, what is the intended MoonBit way to express lookup-based replay/no-op theorems over small transitions?
- If not, could this be relaxed so theorem-style helper functions can talk about lookup results and simple record/method observations like `patch.is_empty()`?
